- **Projects** — each with a 2-line pitch, a screenshot or short GIF, and three links: **live demo, source, README**. Order by strength, best first.
- **About**: 3 sentences, human, with your course and certificate verification number once you have it (Lesson 24).

Build it wherever is fastest in 2026 — GitHub Pages, Carrd, Notion site, or an AI site-builder; the platform is irrelevant, the *working links* are everything. Test every link on your phone. A dead demo link reads as a dead project.

Even with zero-code projects, GitHub is where technical evaluators look — it signals you speak their culture. The minimum viable GitHub:

1. **Real name or consistent handle**, photo, bio with target title ('Building AI agents — n8n, Zapier, LLMs').
2. **One repo per project** — even if the 'code' is mostly JSON exports, prompts, and READMEs. That's legitimate: your prompts, schemas, and test logs *are* the artifacts.
3. **A serious README per repo**: what it does, architecture, screenshots, design decisions, test results, limitations. Pin your best repos.
4. Green squares help but aren't required — a handful of solid repos with excellent READMEs beats a year of commit noise.

Lesson 23's take-home training will feel familiar if take-homes involve repos — many do. You're pre-building that muscle now.

Credibility compounds when everything cross-links. Checklist:

- **Consistent identity**: same name, same photo, same title across LinkedIn, GitHub, and the site — search engines and recruiters both reward coherence.
- **Links everywhere**: LinkedIn Featured → site and repos; site → LinkedIn; every README → live demo; your CV's Projects section → all of it.
- **Working screenshots**: images that load fast and show the *thing working*, not abstract diagrams.
- **Google yourself** (incognito): what actually appears? Fix the top five results you control.

Also set up a professional email on your domain if you have one — `name@yourdomain` beats `name1234` in 2026's trust economy, and it's a 10-minute job.

The site is a living artifact, not a one-time chore. Keep a **build log** — every new project, course milestone, or interesting automation gets a short entry (this pairs perfectly with your Lesson 15 pipeline, which can draft these). Update the site monthly: swap in the newest project, refresh numbers in your results ('12 agents shipped', '40% faster triage'). Small consistent public evidence beats sporadic brilliance — six months of a visible build log is a track record, and a track record is the single most convincing object in the 2026 job market, because it's the one thing that can't be faked in an interview. You've been building one all course. Now it's public.

prompts: Here are my five projects with one-line descriptions: [LIST THEM]. Write the copy for a one-page portfolio: a positioning line, a 2-line pitch per project in priority order with suggested screenshots, and a 3-sentence About. Human tone, no buzzwords.
Review this README like a technical hiring manager deciding in 90 seconds: [PASTE README]. What's missing? What would make me doubt the project is real? Give me the 3 highest-impact fixes.
lessons.exercise: Ship the public layer: one-page portfolio site with all projects linked, GitHub account with a repo and serious README for your best project, consistent identity across all three surfaces, every link tested on mobile. Google yourself in incognito and note what a recruiter sees.

lessons.title: Where AI Jobs Actually Are
lessons.goal: Know the real 2026 AI job map — titles, salary ranges, and where beginners actually get hired — and target the right roles for you.
lessons.audio_intro: Let's replace hype and doom with a map. Yes, the 'prompt engineer' bubble of 2023 partly deflated — it merged into broader roles. But the AI job market of 2026 is bigger, not smaller: every non-tech company now automates, and they hire people who can build agents and pipelines without a computer science degree. In this lesson, Alex lays out the actual titles, what each really does, realistic salary ranges across the US, Israel, and remote, and — most importantly — where beginners genuinely get hired. No fantasy numbers, no doom. Just the map, so you can aim. Salary note upfront: these are directional ranges, not promises; markets vary.

sections.body:
The roles that hire people with *your* skillset:

- **AI Automation Specialist / AI Solutions Engineer** — build agents and pipelines inside companies (n8n, Zapier, APIs). The most open to non-programmers.
- **AI Ops** — keep AI systems running: monitoring, cost control, model routing. Ops people who learn AI are rare and valued.
- **AI Product Manager / AI Product Owner** — decide *what* to automate; needs process fluency more than code.
- **Prompt Engineer / AI Content Specialist** — narrower now, mostly inside marketing, localization, and support-ops teams.
- **AI Consultant / Fractional Automator** — freelance versions of all the above; fastest first dollar.

'AI Engineer' (heavy code) exists too — it's the Python track, not this one, but you'll collaborate with those people constantly.

Directional 2026 figures — markets vary widely, so verify on local listings:

- **United States**: junior AI automation/solutions roles roughly **$70-110k**; mid-level **$110-160k**; AI Ops similar, often higher with on-call pay. Prompt-engineer-flavored roles: **$60-120k** depending on how technical.
- **Israel**: junior automation/AI-ops roles roughly **12-18k ILS/month**; experienced **20-35k ILS/month**; the market is hot and Hebrew/English bilinguals get remote premiums.
- **Remote/global and freelance**: project-based automation from a few hundred dollars per build to $50-150/hour for consultants with a visible portfolio.

The consistent pattern across all three: **portfolio + numbers beats credentials**. Employers test what you built — that's what Module 4 was for.

The entry points that work:

1. **Your current employer** — the #1 path. Volunteer to automate one painful process, ship it, get the title changed or the promotion. Internal converts beat external applicants almost every time.
2. **Small and mid-size companies** — 20-200 people. No AI team, real automation needs, no patience for credentials theater. They hire people who demo working systems.
3. **Agencies and consultancies** — automation boutiques and AI consultancies hire juniors who can build and *communicate*.
3. **Adjacent moves** — support leads becoming AI support specialists; ops people becoming AI Ops; marketers becoming content-automation people. Prior domain + AI skills is the strongest combo in the market.

What rarely works for beginners: applying cold to big-tech 'AI Engineer' roles against CS graduates. Aim where your advantage is real.

sections.h: Reading job descriptions like a pro
sections.body:
Decode postings before applying:

- **Reality check**: 'AI Automation Specialist, must know Python' = hybrid code role. 'n8n/Zapier, workflows, LLM APIs' = your track.
- **Wish-list vs. requirements**: job ads are wish-lists; meet ~60% and apply anyway.
- **Translation table**: 'prompt engineering' → what you did in Module 2. 'RAG experience' → Lesson 14. 'Agent frameworks' → Modules 3-4. 'Stakeholder communication' → your READMEs and test logs.
- **Filter for testability**: postings asking for 'a portfolio or examples of automations built' are *your* postings — they evaluate evidence, not pedigree. Apply to those first.

Build a tracking spreadsheet this week — title, company, source, status, contact. Job search is a pipeline; treat it like one of your projects, with metrics and weekly reviews.

prompts: Here is a job description: [PASTE IT]. Tell me: (1) is this really my track (no-code/low-code automation) or a developer role? (2) which of my five portfolio projects to lead with, (3) the 3 keywords I must mirror in my CV, (4) my honest fit as a % with reasons.

I'm targeting [YOUR CITY/REMOTE + YOUR BACKGROUND]. List the 10 most realistic job titles for me to search for on LinkedIn and job boards, ranked by entry-friendliness for someone with a portfolio but no CS degree. For each, one line on why.
lessons.exercise: Build your job-search pipeline sheet: 15 real open roles that fit your track, sourced from LinkedIn and job boards. For each, note title, salary if listed, the portfolio project you'd lead with, and a fit score. Circle your top 5 — they're your targets for Lessons 22-23 practice.

lessons.title: Interview Prep with an AI Interviewer
lessons.goal: Rehearse the real AI-role interview — story answers, live prompting tests, portfolio walkthroughs — against an AI interviewer until you're smooth.
lessons.audio_intro: Good news you've earned: AI-role interviews are among the most rehearsable in tech, and you own the perfect sparring partner — an AI interviewer that never gets tired, never judges, and can play the skeptical hiring manager, the friendly recruiter, or the technical screener on demand. In this lesson, Alex sets up your practice system: the five question families you'll face, the story format that makes answers land, the portfolio walkthrough you'll deliver, and the live prompting test employers actually give. Then you drill, on record, until smooth. Nerves die with repetition. Let's get you ready to enjoy this.

sections.body:
AI-role interviews circle five families:

1. **Behavioral** — 'tell me about a time you automated something / handled pushback / shipped under uncertainty.'
2. **Technical concepts** — 'explain an agent vs. a workflow,' 'why do LLMs hallucinate,' 'what's RAG?' You've answered all of these in this course.
3. **Live prompting** — 'here's a task, write the prompt' or 'improve this prompt.' Often a shared screen. Module 2 is your muscle memory.
4. **Portfolio deep-dive** — 'walk me through your support agent. Why this escalation rule?' Employers *test* projects — they'll use your demo and probe design decisions.
5. **Scenario/problem-solving** — 'our support queue is drowning; what would you do?' They're testing process thinking: ask questions, propose a pilot, define metrics.

Prepare one story per family and you've covered 80% of any AI interview.

Build your sparring partner in one prompt: 'You are a skeptical but fair interviewer for a [TARGET ROLE] position. Ask one question at a time across these five families, tailored to this job description: [PASTE JD]. After each answer, give feedback: what worked, what was vague, what a stronger candidate would add, then a 1-10 score. Push back at least twice during the interview, like a real hiring manager. Don't let me off easy.' Variants worth running: the **recruiter screen** (fit, motivation, salary — practice your range from Lesson 21), the **technical deep-dive** ('explain function calling to a non-technical stakeholder'), and the **stress test** (hostile follow-ups, 'we tried AI and it failed, convince me'). Three personas, one prompt template each.

sections.h: The story format and the walkthrough
sections.body:
Behavioral answers land with **STAR**: Situation, Task, Action, Result — with your Result lines carrying *numbers* ('cut triage time 40%, 22-case test log, 90% pass rate'). Your Module 4 projects are story goldmines; each one is a ready-made STAR with evidence.

The portfolio walkthrough deserves its own rehearsal — a tight 3-minute tour per project: the problem, the architecture, one hard decision and why, the test results, the limits. Practice with your AI interviewer interrupting you: 'why that escalation rule? what breaks at 10x volume?' Knowing your own READMEs cold — including the limitations you wrote — is what 'tested and real' sounds like. Fumbling your own design decisions is the fastest credibility killer; owning the limits is the fastest credibility *builder*.

The loop that works: **run a full mock interview on record** (voice or video — AI platforms support voice mode; use it, because speaking ≠ typing), **review the transcript**, note every vague answer, hedges ('kind of', 'I guess'), and missed numbers. Patch the weakest answer. Re-run that family only. Repeat. Cadence: 3 full mocks per week, spread out; daily short drills on the shakiest family. Before the real thing: one final mock the day before, then rest — overdrilling the last 12 hours adds nerves, not polish. Also prep your **own questions** for them (what does success look like in 90 days? how do you decide what to automate next?) — interviews are two-directional, and good questions read as seniority.

prompts: You are a skeptical hiring manager interviewing me for [TARGET ROLE]. Job description: [PASTE JD]. One question at a time across behavioral, technical concepts, live prompting, portfolio deep-dive, and scenario families. After each answer: feedback + score out of 10 + one pushback follow-up. My portfolio: [1-LINE PER PROJECT]. Do not go easy on me.

Here is my answer to 'walk me through your favorite project': [PASTE OR DICTATE]. Rewrite it as a tight 3-minute walkthrough: problem, architecture, one hard decision with reasoning, test results with numbers, honest limits. Then give me the 3 questions a technical interviewer would ask about it.
lessons.exercise: Run three full recorded mock interviews this week with your AI interviewer — one per persona (recruiter, hiring manager, technical). Review each recording, patch your two weakest answers, and re-drill just those families. Save your best 3-minute project walkthrough as written notes you can review before any real interview.

lessons.title: Take-Home Assignments — and How to Crush Them
lessons.goal: Handle AI-role take-home tests professionally — scoping, building, documenting, and presenting so evaluators can't help but be impressed.
lessons.audio_intro: The final gate before most AI-role offers: the take-home. 'Build us a small agent that does X. You have five days.' Some candidates panic and over-build; others submit something that doesn't run. You will do neither — because a take-home is just a Module 4 project with a deadline, and you have four of those plus a system for building them. In this lesson, Alex covers the whole lifecycle: reading the brief for what's actually being tested, scoping ruthlessly, the README that does half your pitching, the demo that proves it runs, and how to present your decisions like a professional. Also: your rights — time budgets and when to push back. Let's crush it.

sections.h: Reading the brief: what's really tested
sections.body:
Take-homes almost never test raw skill alone — they test **judgment under a deadline**. Decode the brief before touching a tool:

- **The explicit ask**: build X with Y constraints. Underline the constraints — they're the grading rubric.
- **The implicit tests**: usually three — can you scope realistically? do you document decisions? does it actually run?
- **The realistic effort**: ask! 'How many hours do you expect candidates to spend?' is a senior-sounding question, not a weak one. If they say 3 hours, submitting 20 hours of work signals you can't scope — a real failure mode.

Then decide your **intentional scope**: what you'll build, what you'll stub, what you'll list as 'given more time.' Evaluators love a visible `future-work.md` more than an overbuilt mess.

sections.h: The build: your Module 4 system, on a clock
sections.body:
This is why Module 4 existed — take-homes are typically mini versions of your portfolio: a support agent, a RAG demo, a pipeline. Run your known-good loop, timeboxed:

- **Hour 1**: skeleton and the riskiest part first — if the core won't work, you want to know in hour one, not hour nine.
- **Middle hours**: build the smallest complete version that satisfies every explicit requirement. Complete-but-small beats impressive-but-broken, every time.
- **Final third**: testing (your test-set habit — even 10 cases puts you ahead of most candidates) and the README.

Non-negotiable: **it must run on their machine.** Include exact setup steps, a working demo link, and zero 'it worked on my machine' energy. That sentence has ended candidacies.

sections.h: The README is half your grade
sections.body:
Evaluators read the README before or instead of the code. Use your proven structure:

- **Problem and approach** in three sentences, human-readable.
- **What I built / what I deliberately didn't** — your scope decisions, stated proudly.
- **How to run it** — numbered, tested on a clean machine (or a live link).
- **Design decisions** — 'I chose X over Y because Z.' This is where judgment becomes visible and gradeable.
- **Testing** — your test set and results table.
- **Given more time** — 3 bullets. Shows vision plus discipline.

This is the exact README you've written four times. The take-home rewards exactly the habits you now have. Screenshots and a 60-90 second demo video complete the package — evaluators who feel the demo *work* in two minutes are already on your side.

Many processes end with a walkthrough call. Structure it like your Lesson 22 project tour: problem, approach, one decision story, demo, limits, future work — 5-7 minutes, then invite questions. Expect 'why didn't you…' questions: they test composure, not perfection; 'I considered it and deprioritized it because of the time budget — here's where it would slot in' is a *great* answer. 

And know your rights: a take-home shouldn't exceed roughly 4-8 hours or solve a company's *current real business problem unpaid. If it smells like free work — real data, production scope, no compensation — it's fair to ask about it, or walk. Companies that respect candidates design respectful take-homes; the assignment is often your first look at how they actually operate.

prompts: Here is a take-home brief: [PASTE BRIEF]. Give me: (1) what's likely being tested beyond the explicit ask, (2) a ruthless scope plan for a [X]-hour budget — build / stub / skip, (3) the 3 risks that could sink it and how to de-risk each early, (4) 5 clarifying questions worth asking before starting.
Review my take-home README like the evaluator: [PASTE README]. Where would I lose points? What's missing? What sentence should I add? Do not rewrite it — give me the fix list.
lessons.exercise: Do a timed drill: find a realistic take-home brief (or generate one with AI: 'write a 4-hour take-home for an AI Automation Specialist role'), then execute the full lifecycle in one sitting — scoped build, test set, README, 60-second demo video. Review: where did the time actually go? Fix your process while it's cheap.

sections.body: Your capstone combines everything: build an agent that runs a real part of your week. Minimum scope: **(1) inbox triage** (Lesson 12's read-only digest), **(2) calendar proposals** (reads availability, suggests slots, human confirms), **(3) document work** (summarize attachments, extract key fields to a sheet — reuse your Lesson 16 cleaning skills), **(4) a daily briefing** — one message each morning: today's meetings, priority emails, open tasks. Architecture: your platform's agent node, a system message with all six blocks, the smallest safe toolset, guardrails from Lesson 12 (read-only where possible, human fence on anything irreversible), and a change/action log. Keep it running for at least five days — real usage data is your results section, and 'I use it daily' is the strongest sentence in any interview.

The completion exam checks working knowledge across all six modules:

- **M1**: how LLMs work, context windows, hallucination categories and verification workflow.
- **M2**: structured-output schemas, few-shot design, when reasoning pays, system-message blocks.
- **M3**: the agent loop, tools and function calling concepts, permission and safety design.
- **M4**: the anatomy of your five projects — what you built and the decisions you made.
- **M5**: CV keywords and tailoring, LinkedIn zones, portfolio evidence.
- **M6**: the job map, interview families, take-home lifecycle.

Format: multiple choice plus short practicals — write a schema, diagnose a broken prompt, spot the hallucination risk. It's open-notes and open-internet, like real work. Study method: reread your own project READMEs and exercise notes; you wrote the exam's answers already, in your own words.

Submit the following, complete — partial submissions bounce:

1. **Final project link or repo** — live demo (or screen recording), source, README with architecture, guardrails, five-day usage log, and your design decisions.
2. **Test log** — minimum 10-message test set with results, including escalation and failure cases.
3. **Exam completion** — passed within the allowed attempts (you get retakes; treat them as feedback, not failure).
4. **Portfolio readiness check** — your Lesson 20 site updated with all five projects, links tested.
5. **Reflection** — 150 words: what you built, what you'd improve, what you'll automate next.

Timeline: most finish project five and the exam within one to two weeks of reaching this lesson. The certificate with its **verification number** is issued after all five items pass review — the number is what turns the certificate from a PDF into a checkable claim.

Certified, five tested projects, a public portfolio — now run the machine you built in Module 5 and 6: tailored applications to your Lesson 21 target list, weekly mock interviews, weekly posts from your content pipeline. Keep the assistant agent running; keep a build log; interviewers ask 'what have you automated lately?' and you'll have a same-week answer. The field will keep changing — the course's own method (AI builds, AI teaches, you verify) is your method now too: when a new model or tool lands, build a small thing with it, test it like Lesson 4 taught you, write the README. That loop — build, test, document, show — is the career. Verification number in hand, go claim the jobs. — Alex, signing off.

Then claim your certificate and verification number — and put that number on your CV and LinkedIn the same day.
